No classes here! Why, that is idle talk. The village beau sneers at the country boor; The importuning mendicants who walk Our cites’ streets despise the parish poor. The daily toiler at some noisy loom Holds back her garments from the kitchen aid. Meanwhile the latter leans upon her broom, Unconscious of the bow the laundress made. The grocer’s daughter eyes the farmer’s lass With haughty glances; and the lawyer’s wife Would pay no visits to the trading class, If policy were not her creed in life. The merchant’s son nods coldly at the clerk; The proud possessor of a pedigree Ignores the youth whose father rose by work; The title-seeking maiden scorns all three. The aristocracy of blood looks down Upon the “nouveau riche”; and in disdain, The lovers of the intellectual frown On both, and worship at the shrine of brain. “No classes here,” the clergyman has said; “We are one family.” Yet see his rage And horror when his favorite son would wed Some pure and pretty player on the stage. It is the vain but natural way Of vaunting our weak selves, our pride, our worth! Not till the long delayed millennial day Shall we behold “no classes” on God’s earth.

outputs.L1:
**No Classes Here**

No classes here! Why, that is idle talk.
The village beau derides the country boor;
The clamoring mendicants who walk
Our city streets look down upon the poor.

The daily toiler at some noisy loom
Withholds her skirts from her the kitchen aid,
While she, in turn, leans idle on her broom,
Unmindful of the bow the laundress made.

The grocer's daughter eyes the farmer's lass
With haughty scorn; the lawyer's stately wife
Would deign no visit to the trading class,
Were policy not her sole creed in life.

The merchant's son nods coldly at the clerk;
The proud possessor of a pedigree
Disdains the youth whose father rose by work;
The title-seeking maiden scorns all three.

The aristocracy of blood looks down
Upon the "nouveau riche"; and, in disdain,
The lovers of the intellect will frown
On both, and worship at the shrine of brain.

"No classes here," the clergyman has said;
"We are one family." Yet mark his rage
And horror when his favorite son would wed
Some pure and comely player on the stage.

It is the vain, yet all too human way
Of vaunting our weak selves—our pride, our worth!
Not till the long-delayed millennial day
Shall we behold "no classes" on God's earth.

---

I preserved the original meaning, structure, and rhyme scheme while refining word choices for smoother flow and heightened eloquence (e.g., "derides," "clamoring," "Withholds," "Unmindful," "deign," "mark his rage," "all too human way"). Would you like a version that adheres even more strictly to the original wording, or one that departs more freely?
outputs.L2:
There's no such thing as a classless society here—such notions are merely foolish chatter. The stylish young man of the town looks down his nose at the rustic countryman, while the persistent beggars roaming through our city streets hold contempt for the poor of the parish. A woman working all day at a clattering loom pulls her clothing away so it won't touch the kitchen helper. That helper, meanwhile, rests against her broom, never noticing the greeting the laundry worker offered her.

The girl who works in the grocery casts snobbish looks at the farmer's daughter. A lawyer's wife wouldn't bother calling on anyone in trade, except that she treats social strategy as her guiding principle. A merchant's son gives the clerk only a chilly nod. Someone who boasts of noble ancestry pays no attention to a young man whose father climbed up through hard labor—and the young woman chasing after a title looks down on all three of them.

Those born into aristocratic bloodlines sneer at the newly wealthy. Meanwhile, people who prize intellect look down scornfully on both groups, devoting themselves entirely to the worship of the mind.

"We have no classes here," declares the minister; "we're all one big family." Yet watch how furious and appalled he becomes when his beloved son wishes to marry an innocent, lovely actress from the theater.

This is simply our foolish yet natural tendency—to puff up our feeble selves, our vanity, our sense of our own importance. Only when the long-awaited age of divine peace finally arrives will we ever witness a world with "no classes" upon God's earth.
outputs.L3:
# The Persistence of Class Distinctions in Society

Class distinctions permeate every level of society, creating an intricate web of social hierarchy that touches nearly all human interactions. At its core, this system operates on a simple but troubling principle: each social group habitually looks down upon those it perceives as occupying a lower rung on the social ladder. This pattern of condescension is not confined to the upper echelons of society but extends throughout its entire structure.

Perhaps most revealing is how even the poor and lowly participate enthusiastically in this hierarchy, despite having so little themselves. Beggars, who possess almost nothing, still find reason to scorn the parish poor, drawing distinctions where an outsider might see none. Similarly, servants—themselves in positions of subordination—maintain their own elaborate systems of rank, observing petty status distinctions among their fellow workers with remarkable care. This demonstrates that the impulse toward social differentiation exists independently of one's actual position in society.

The competition for social superiority takes many forms, and these different claims to distinction often stand in tension with one another. Aristocratic blood, with its appeal to ancestry and inheritance, competes against newly acquired wealth, which asserts its own kind of legitimacy through material success. Meanwhile, intellectual achievement offers yet another basis for claiming elevated status. Each of these forms of superiority jostles for recognition, revealing that there is no single, agreed-upon measure of social worth.

The hypocrisy underlying these attitudes becomes strikingly apparent in certain revealing moments. Consider the clergyman who preaches the comforting doctrine that "we are one family," suggesting a fundamental equality among all people. Yet this noble sentiment is exposed as hollow when he reacts with genuine horror at the prospect of his son marrying a virtuous stage performer. Despite her moral character, her profession places her beneath his family in his estimation—demonstrating that his professed belief in human brotherhood collapses the moment it threatens his own social standing.

Ultimately, this pervasive tendency to assert our superiority over others springs from deep-seated human vanity and pride. These are not superficial flaws easily corrected but fundamental features of human nature that manifest across all social contexts. Given this reality, true classlessness remains an elusive ideal—one that may only be realized in some distant, idealized future, if it can be achieved at all. Until human beings overcome their innate desire to elevate themselves above their fellows, the divisions of class will likely endure in one form or another.
outputs.L4:
# On the Persistence of Class

The poem takes as its central target a comfortable modern illusion: the notion that we have somehow achieved, or are on the verge of achieving, a classless society. Against this cheerful claim, the poet marshals evidence drawn from ordinary life, constructing an elaborate chain of social contempt in which every group, no matter how humble or exalted, finds someone beneath it to disdain.

The catalogue begins at the bottom of the conventional social ladder and works its way upward, though the poem's irony lies in showing that no rung is free of the same failing. Villagers look askance at those they consider rougher or poorer than themselves. Laborers, in turn, draw their own distinctions, measuring dignity by trade or wage. The merchants, proud of their commerce and their accumulated wealth, regard the working hands as lesser beings. Above them, the aristocrats hold the merchants in polite contempt, dismissing new money and the taint of trade as beneath their inherited grace.

Nor are the educated and the pious exempt. The intellectuals, confident in the superiority of the mind, look down upon aristocrat and laborer alike, imagining that learning confers a special rank. And even the clergy, who might be expected to preach a common humanity before God, are shown to harbor their own quiet condescensions, setting themselves apart as guardians of a higher truth.

What emerges from this survey is a diagnosis rather than a mere complaint. Class distinction, the poem argues, is not fundamentally a matter of economics or accident of birth; it springs from something rooted deep in human nature itself—from vanity and pride. Each person, hungry for a sense of worth, secures it by locating others below him. The instinct to rank and to look down is universal, and so the hierarchy reproduces itself endlessly, from the poorest village up to the most refined circles of learning and faith.

The poem's conclusion follows logically from this insight. If class arises from the prideful heart of humanity, then no political reform or social program can abolish it; the problem lies too deep for such remedies. A genuinely classless world, the poet suggests, will not arrive through human effort at all. It belongs instead to an idealized future—a millennial age, when human nature itself is at last transformed and the vanity that divides us is finally overcome. Until that distant day, the poem implies, the boast of a classless society remains a hollow and self-flattering fiction.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about how class divisions and social snobbery persist in every level of society, even among those who claim there are "no classes."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Egalitarians

They gathered in their circle, proud,
And spoke of leveling the ground,
"No masters here, no bending crowd,
No pedigrees, no titles crowned."

Yet watch them measure, glance to glance,
The cut of cloth, the turn of speech,
Who reads the proper books, perchance,
Who holds the values each must reach.

The one who spoke too plain was pitied,
The one who spoke too fine was scorned,
And subtle hierarchies fitted
Where every equal soul was born.

They traded titles old for new—
Not "Lord" and "Sir," but "one of us,"
And drew their careful lines askew
Round who deserved the sacred trust.

For in the meeting hall of saints
Who preached that all division ends,
The sharpest pen still drew constraints:
The circle of the proper friends.

So mark it well in every age,
On palace floor or commune's stone:
The human heart will build its cage
And name some soil more pure its own.

The duke looks down upon the clerk,
The clerk upon the man who begs,
The one who's free of both their work
Still climbs upon another's legs.

And those who cry the loudest, "None
Shall stand above his fellow man!"
Have only shuffled, one by one,
The rankings by a newer plan.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming poem in the style of Ella Wheeler Wilcox titled "No Classes."
counterfactuals.output:
# No Classes

There is no class the poor may hold,
No rank the humble soul may claim,
Save what the honest heart makes bold,
And what the striving spirit's flame.

The palace and the cottage door
Both open to the self-same sky;
The rich man and the toiling poor
Alike shall live, alike shall die.

No crest of gold, no titled name,
Can lift one grain of common dust;
The soul that dares the world's acclaim
Must build its greatness on its trust.

For nature knows no high, no low,
No lord to serve, no serf to be;
She bids the same warm sunlight flow
On king and slave, on bond and free.

The blossom in the wayside sod
Wears beauty rich as garden rose;
And in the humblest child of God
A kingly heart may find repose.

Then let us cast our pride away,
And clasp the hand that labor worns;
For brotherhood shall win the day,
And love outlast the crowns and thorns.

We all are children of one breath,
One dawn, one darkness at the last;
And equal in the arms of death,
When all our little pomp is passed.

So hold your head, though low your birth,
And meet the great with fearless eyes—
There are no classes on this earth
Save honest hearts and honest lies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical Victorian-style poem showing how each social rank looks down on the one below it, from aristocrats to laborers.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Great Chain of Sneering

*A Satire in the Victorian Mode*

---

The Duke surveys his marble hall,
And sniffs at Barons, one and all:
"Such lesser blood! Such recent peers!
Their titles date but hundred years."

The Baron, polished, proud, and stout,
Regards the Merchant with a pout:
"He *earns*, the wretch—how very crude!
To touch a coin is frightful rude."

The Merchant, counting up his gold,
Finds shopkeepers a sight to scold:
"They haggle over pence and crown!
Such vulgar folk should keep their town."

The Shopkeeper, in apron neat,
Looks down upon the workman's street:
"He labours with his back, poor clod,
While I keep ledgers, thank the Lord."

The Craftsman, skilled in wood and brass,
Disdains the digging labouring class:
"He merely *sweats*—what artless toil!
I *shape* the world; he moves the soil."

The Labourer, with blistered hand,
Surveys the beggar where he stands:
"At least I work! This idle thief
Would rather starve than seek relief."

The Beggar, ragged, in the cold,
Eyes stray dogs with contempt untold:
"A cur! A brute! It cannot pray—
Thank Heaven *I'm* a man today."

And God above, so I am told,
Surveyed this pageant, proud and cold,
Then turned to Gabriel with a sigh:
"They've learned to sneer. And so have I."

---

*Thus every rung upon the stair*
*Looks down to find some soul to bear*
*The weight of scorn it can't abide—*
*So spins the wheel of English pride.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem that critiques the hypocrisy of people who say everyone is equal while still practicing their own forms of snobbery?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Egalitarians

They toast to equal worth for all
With crystal raised in marble halls,
Then wince to hear a neighbor speak
In accents from the working week.

"We're all the same," they gently preach,
While quietly they choose the beach
No common family can afford—
Equality, but not the horde.

They love mankind in the abstract,
A principle they won't retract,
Yet cross the street, avert the eye,
When flesh-and-blood inconveniences pass by.

Their bumper stickers cry for peace,
Their gated fences never cease;
They'll champion the poor by name
Then judge the poor who look the same.

The self they scorn in others' pride
Sits comfortably, warmed inside—
For snobbery wears many gowns,
And virtue makes the finest crowns.

So here's the oldest human art:
To hold two mansions in one heart—
One built of words where all are kin,
One walled, with guest lists locked within.

---

I aimed to skewer the *specific* gap between stated ideals and lived behavior, rather than dismissing the ideal of equality itself. Would you like a version with a different tone—angrier, more satirical, or perhaps turned inward as self-critique?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a long poem in iambic pentameter about pride, class distinctions, and the illusion of a classless society, ending with a hopeful note about a future millennial day.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Painted Equal Day**

When morning gilds the spires above the town,
The wealthy walk with slow and measured tread;
They wear their fortune like a golden crown
And climb the stairs where humbler men have bled.

For pride is patient, dressed in silk and lace,
It smiles from carriages of burnished gold,
And bids the ragged keep their proper place
Beneath the wheels, in gutters wet and cold.

The lord surveys his acres, wide and green,
And thinks the poor were fashioned for his gain;
He never sees the toil that goes unseen,
The bending backs, the harvest bought with pain.

"There are no classes here," the great ones cry,
"We all are equal underneath the sun."
Yet who has ever heard the beggar's sigh
Reach ears of those whose easy day is done?

The illusion glitters like a pane of glass,
A mirror where the mighty preen and gaze;
It tells them all men freely rise and pass
Through open doors to bright and equal days.

But doors are locked with keys of ancient name,
And gates are guarded well by rank and gold;
The poor may knock, and knock, and knock the same,
Yet stand outside forever in the cold.

The scholar's son is groomed for lofty halls,
The laborer's for the furnace and the mill;
And what men call their freedom, when it falls,
Is but the freedom of another's will.

Oh, proud pretense of one united throng!
The banquet's spread, but few may take a seat;
The many sing the powerful their song
And gather up the crumbs beneath their feet.

Yet listen—in the alley and the field,
A murmur rises, low but growing strong;
The hearts of those who labor will not yield
Their ancient dream of righting ancient wrong.

For something in the human breast rebels
Against the chains that custom calls its due;
It hears within the poorest hovel's cells
A whisper that the world might yet be new.

Not new with pride reversed, nor hate for hate,
Nor beggar throned where lord was throned before,
But cleansed of all the walls that men create
To keep their brothers strangers at the door.

Then let the false equality dissolve,
That painted mask upon a hollow face,
And let a truer union take resolve
To lift, not level down, the human race.

I see it dimly, as a distant shore
Beyond the storms of this dividing sea:
A day when pride and pomp shall be no more,
And every soul at last be truly free.

When bread is shared as freely as the air,
And none shall starve while others idly dine;
When toil and rest fall evenly and fair,
And every child may drink the equal wine.

That millennial dawn shall surely break,
Though we who dream may never see it rise;
For those who follow, let us stay awake
And keep the promise burning in our eyes.

So sing, my heart, against the present night,
And labor on though weary and alone;
The dawn shall come, the future breaks in light,
And every man shall come into his own.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
